sizes.title: Social image sizes
sizes.intro: Open Graph images are served at 1200 × 630 pixels — a 1.91:1 ratio that Facebook, LinkedIn and Slack all crop to. Most platforms accept that single image, but a few use their own ratio, so it is worth knowing where the differences are before you commit to one asset.

rows.og: The safe default. One 1200 × 630 image covers Facebook, LinkedIn and Slack link unfurls.
rows.x-large: Used when your page declares twitter:card as summary_large_image. Near-identical to Open Graph, so the same file works.
rows.x-summary: The small square card. X falls back to this when no large-image card is declared.
rows.pinterest: Vertical by design. A 1.91:1 image is heavily letterboxed here, so generate a separate asset if Pinterest matters.
rows.whatsapp: Thumbnails are cropped to a square. Keep the important content centred or it will be cut off.

limits.title: Limits and gotchas
limits.file-size: Keep the file under 5 MB. Facebook accepts up to 8 MB, but X rejects anything larger than 5 MB.
limits.formats: Use PNG or JPG. SVG is not supported by any major crawler, and WebP support is inconsistent.
limits.text-safe-area: Keep text within the central 80% of the frame. Different platforms crop the edges by different amounts.
limits.retina: Do not upscale beyond 1200 × 630. Platforms downscale for display, and larger files slow down the first unfurl.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.intro: Most Open Graph problems are caching or URL issues rather than problems with the image itself.

cache.problem: The preview still shows the old image
cache.fix: Platforms cache aggressively. Force a re-scrape with the Facebook Sharing Debugger, the X Card Validator, or LinkedIn's Post Inspector. Changing the image URL also works.

absolute-url.fix: og:image must be an absolute URL including the scheme and host. Relative paths such as /og.png are ignored by every crawler.

blocked.problem: The image works in a browser but not when shared
blocked.fix: Check that the image is not behind authentication, a paywall, or a robots.txt rule. Crawlers fetch it anonymously.

missing-dimensions.problem: The card renders small or reflows after a moment
missing-dimensions.fix: Declare og:image:width and og:image:height. Without them the platform must download the image before it can size the card.

format.problem: The image is blank or corrupt on one platform only
format.fix: Re-export as PNG or JPG. WebP and AVIF are still unevenly supported, and animated formats are never used for previews.

robots-txt.title: robots.txt Validator
robots-txt.description: Paste a robots.txt or fetch one from a URL. See the parsed rules, get the syntax checked, and test whether any path is blocked for a given crawler.

fetchErrors.invalidUrl: That does not look like a valid site URL.
fetchErrors.blockedHost: That host is not publicly reachable, so it cannot be fetched.
fetchErrors.redirected: The request was redirected. Enter the final domain directly.
fetchErrors.tooLarge: That robots.txt is too large to fetch.
fetchErrors.fetchFailed: Could not fetch robots.txt from that site.

tester.title: Test a URL
tester.noRule: No rule matched, so the path is allowed
tester.noGroup: No group applies to this crawler, so everything is allowed

issues.title: Checks
issues.bom: The file begins with a byte-order mark, which some crawlers read as part of the first directive.
issues.missingColon: This line has no colon, so it is not a directive.
issues.ruleBeforeUserAgent: This rule appears before any User-agent line, so no crawler will apply it.
issues.sitemapNotAbsolute: Sitemap must be an absolute URL including the protocol.
issues.crawlDelayInvalid: Crawl-delay must be a non-negative number.
issues.crawlDelayIgnoredByGoogle: Google ignores Crawl-delay. Use the crawl rate setting in Search Console instead.
issues.noindexUnsupported: Google stopped supporting noindex in robots.txt in 2019. Use a meta robots tag or an X-Robots-Tag header.
issues.hostNonStandard: Host is non-standard and ignored by Google.
issues.blocksEntireSite: This blocks every crawler from the whole site.
issues.noSitemap: No Sitemap directive. Adding one helps crawlers find your URLs.

overview.title: What robots.txt does and does not do
overview.description: robots.txt tells well-behaved crawlers which paths to avoid requesting. It is a crawling instruction, not an access control and not an indexing instruction. A blocked URL can still appear in search results if other pages link to it — Google just will not have read the page. To keep something out of the index, use a noindex meta tag on a page that is crawlable, or protect it properly with authentication.

matching.title: How path matching works
matching.description: Matching is prefix-based and case-sensitive. Two wildcards are supported: * matches any run of characters and $ anchors the end of the URL.

precedence.title: Which rule wins
precedence.description: When several rules match, the most specific one wins — that is, the one with the longest path pattern. If an Allow and a Disallow are the same length, Allow wins. This is why Allow: /folder/public overrides Disallow: /folder/ for a URL underneath it.
precedence.example: Given Disallow: /folder/ and Allow: /folder/public, the path /folder/public/page is allowed because the Allow pattern is longer.

groups.title: How groups work
groups.description: Consecutive User-agent lines share one group of rules. A crawler uses the single group whose user-agent token matches it most specifically, and ignores every other group — including the * group. That is the most common robots.txt mistake: adding a Googlebot group and assuming Googlebot still obeys the rules under *.

blockAll.fix: This blocks the entire site. It is the single most common cause of a site vanishing from search after a launch.

groupInheritance.problem: Expecting a named crawler to also follow the * rules
groupInheritance.fix: It will not. Repeat any shared rules inside the named group.

noindex.problem: Using Disallow to remove a page from search
noindex.fix: Blocked pages can still be indexed from external links. Allow crawling and serve a noindex tag instead.

blockedAssets.fix: Google renders pages before ranking them. Blocking assets can make a page look broken to the crawler.

relativeSitemap.fix: Sitemap must be an absolute URL, including https://.
